title: The foot measures the shoe
hook: the body is the measure of what you need, as the foot is of the shoe (Enchiridion 39)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hēgemonikon, the ruling mind, guarded like a foot on a garage floor. Your line was a beat before agreeing.

Open a closet and count the shoes. Not to judge. Just count. Then count your feet. Two, for most people. Somewhere between those two numbers there's a story. A pair for running. Then a nicer pair for running. Then a pair that matches the jacket. Epictetus, who by tradition lived with very little, looked at the humble shoe and saw a whole philosophy of having. Section thirty-nine is short.
screen: `COUNT THE SHOES.` → `NOW COUNT YOUR FEET.` → `THE FOOT MEASURES THE SHOE.`

segments.voice: The body, Epictetus says, is the measure of what each person needs to own, as the foot is the measure of the shoe. A shoe has a job, and the foot tells you when it's done. Food, clothing, shelter: the body tells you, roughly, how much is enough. Stop there, he says, and you'll keep the measure. Step past it, and you'll be carried along as if over a cliff. Past the measure, there's no natural place to stop. He tells the slide with a shoe. Once you go beyond what the foot needs, the shoe becomes gilded, then purple, then embroidered. Hear the ladder in those three words: plain leather becomes a show. Each step makes sense once you've taken the one before it, and nothing on the ladder ever says that's enough. Why is the body such a good measure? It comes with you. It doesn't read advertisements. It gets full, it gets warm, it gets dry, and then it's done. Desire has no such signal. Epicurus, who led a rival school, made a similar point in his own way: what nature needs is limited and easy to get, while what empty opinion wants has no limit. Two schools, each with its own reasons, pointing at the same quiet fact. Enough is a real thing.
screen: `THE BODY IS THE MEASURE OF HAVING.` · `PAST IT, OVER A CLIFF.` · `GILDED, THEN PURPLE, THEN EMBROIDERED.` · `THE BODY KNOWS ENOUGH; DESIRE DOESN'T.` · then, large: `THE FOOT MEASURES.`

segments.voice: Feel your feet where they rest, the clothes on your body, the seat under you; for this minute, the body has what it needs. Think of one thing you own more than enough of, or one thing you've been wanting that the body isn't asking for, and just notice it. Then come back to your feet, and to the plain feeling of enough.
Epicurus. The rival teacher who said what nature needs is limited and easy to get; the body is the measure of what you need to own. Today's word.
Your line: the foot measures. The foot already knows where enough is. Day three hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism use the body's actual needs as a measure for buying and owning, and notice when a want has gone past what the body asks for.

sources.ref: Epicurus, Principal Doctrines 15 (natural wealth is limited)

notes: Enchiridion 39 paraphrased: the body is the measure of possession to each, as the foot of the shoe; keep to it and you keep the measure; pass it and you are carried as down a precipice; the shoe becomes gilded, then purple, then embroidered. Confirm order of the three.
Tyrian purple from murex sea snails, associated with emperors: standard; confirm.
Epicurus, Principal Doctrines 15 (and Letter to Menoeceus): natural wealth is limited and easily procured, the wealth of vain opinion extends to infinity. Paraphrased; confirm.
'As far as we know owned very little': Epictetus' simple living is reported (e.g., Simplicius; the iron lamp anecdote in Discourses 1.18). Confirm phrasing.
